context_blurb:
The ground under your feet is moving. Earth's stiff outer shell is cracked into giant slabs called plates, which creep along, carrying continents and sea floor. Where they part, collide or grind past each other, they build mountains and oceans and shake the land with earthquakes.

A plate is the crust plus the top of the mantle, the thick layer of hot rock below. Most plates move a few centimetres a year, from about one to ten, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow. GPS receivers fixed to bedrock measure the creep, and at five centimetres a year a plate travels fifty kilometres in a million years.

Heat from radioactive atoms deep inside Earth, and heat left from its birth, keep the mantle's solid rock churning very slowly, hot rock rising and cooler rock sinking. A plate's old, cold edge sinking back into the mantle is part of that churning, and its weight drags the plate along: the strongest force on a plate, far ahead of the push from the ocean ridges.

Where two plates move apart, hot mantle rock rises into the gap and partly melts. The magma, or melted rock, fills the crack and hardens into new ocean crust, so new sea floor is made there. This has built the mid-ocean ridge, Earth's longest mountain chain, which stands high because its new rock is still hot and swollen.

A plate can also split on land, opening a rift valley, a long sunken valley shaken by earthquakes and volcanoes. Over millions of years the valley floor sinks until the sea floods in, and magma welling up between the halves becomes the floor of a new ocean. The Red Sea is a young ocean opening this way.

Earth grows no bigger for all that new floor, because old sea floor sinks back into the mantle at the trenches, the ocean's deepest gashes, as fast as new floor forms at the ridges. Some geologists once argued that Earth must be swelling like a balloon, but in 2011 a NASA-led team under Xiaoping Wu measured Earth from space and found no measurable growth.

Density is how much mass is packed into a given space, and ocean rock is denser than the lighter rock of a continent, growing colder and denser still with age. So where ocean floor meets a continent, the ocean plate goes under, though its crust is actually the thinner of the two.

An island arc, a curved chain of volcanic islands beside a deep trench, marks a place where one ocean plate sinks beneath another. Water carried down with the sinking plate helps the hot rock above it melt, and the melted rock rises to build the islands, many of them active at once.

When the ocean between two continents has sunk away, they collide. Continental rock is too light to sink deep, so neither side goes under; instead the crust crumples, folds and stacks up to about twice its usual thickness, raising a range of high, folded mountains. The Himalayas rose this way.

Along California's San Andreas Fault, plates grind sideways past each other. The plates keep creeping, but friction locks the fault, the crack between them, so the rock on each side slowly bends and stores energy, like a stick bent in two hands. When this stress, the force building in the rock, grows too great, the fault slips all at once and the rock snaps back: an earthquake. Harry Fielding Reid worked this out from the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, which split a fence across the fault and shifted its halves some 2.6 metres.

Some volcanoes rise far from plate edges, over a hot spot, where unusually hot rock wells up from deep in the mantle. The hot spot stays nearly still and builds a volcano on the plate above; the plate carries that volcano off, and a new one grows in its place. In Hawaii the Pacific Plate creeps north-west, so the youngest island, which erupts most, lies at the chain's south-east end, and the islands grow older toward the north-west.

Plot the world's strong earthquakes and active volcanoes on a map, and most fall in narrow belts along the edges of Earth's plates, where the rigid slabs do their grinding, sinking and pulling apart. Many coasts, such as the Atlantic's, sit inside a plate and stay quiet. Young mountain belts follow plate edges too, while old ranges like the Appalachians now sit inside a plate.
